title: Ὅπλα καὶ ἀγορή
about: Dawn rises and Thetis reaches the ships with Hephaestus’ armour, to find Achilles lying over the body of Patroclus. She takes his hand, tells him to let the dead man lie and to receive the arms, and sets them down before him; the Myrmidons shrink from the sight, but Achilles’ anger only grows, and he looks on the gifts with delight. He fears that flies will breed maggots in Patroclus’ wounds, and Thetis promises to keep the body sound for a year or more, tells him to call the assembly and renounce his wrath against Agamemnon, and fills him with strength and drips ambrosia and nectar into Patroclus. Achilles goes along the shore crying out, and even the helmsmen and stewards come to the assembly, with the wounded Diomedes, Odysseus and Agamemnon last. Achilles speaks first, wishing Artemis had killed the girl at the ships on the day he took Lyrnessus, owning that the quarrel has helped only Hector and the Trojans, and ending his anger: let the Achaeans be urged to war.

sentences.t:
Ἠὼς μὲν κροκόπεπλος ἀπ’ Ὠκεανοῖο ῥοάων
ὄρνυθ’, ἵν’ ἀθανάτοισι φόως φέροι ἠδὲ βροτοῖσιν·
sentences.l:
Dawn, saffron-robed, for her part, from the streams of Oceanus
was rising, so that to the immortals she might bring light, and to mortals;
sentences.i: Dawn in her saffron robe rose from the streams of Oceanus, to bring light to the immortals and to mortals alike;
sentences.n: Book 19 opens at dawn, with Dawn rising from the streams of Oceanus, the river that rings the world. κροκόπεπλος ‘saffron-robed’ is the stock epithet of Dawn and is translated every time, and the second line is the second line of the Odyssey’s dawn-formula (5.2) except that the Odyssey has the augmented ὤρνυθ’ (the Iliad’s own dawn at 11.2 has this form, ending βροτοῖσι); in both places Dawn rises from the bed of Tithonus, not from the streams of Oceanus. ὄρνυθ’ is ὄρνυτο, the unaugmented imperfect middle of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’, so ‘was rising’; ἵνα with the optative φέροι gives purpose, ‘so that she might bring’. Ὠκεανοῖο has the epic ending -οιο and ῥοάων is the epic genitive plural of ῥοή ‘stream’. μέν ‘for her part’ is answered by the δέ of line 3.

sentences.t: ἣ δ’ ἐς νῆας ἵκανε θεοῦ πάρα δῶρα φέρουσα.
sentences.l: And she to the ships came, from the god bearing gifts.
sentences.i: while she came to the ships, bringing gifts from the god.
sentences.n: ἣ δ’ is Thetis, set against Dawn by μέν … δέ; the god is Hephaestus, whose armour she brings, as the last lines of Book 18 told. ἵκανε is the imperfect of ἱκάνω ‘come’. θεοῦ πάρα is παρὰ θεοῦ with the accent drawn back, because the preposition follows its noun, and means ‘from the god’; δῶρα φέρουσα ‘bearing gifts’ is a present participle.

sentences.t:
εὗρε δὲ Πατρόκλῳ περικείμενον ὃν φίλον υἱὸν
κλαίοντα λιγέως·
sentences.l:
And she found, lying round Patroclus, her own dear son
weeping clearly;
sentences.i: She found her own dear son lying round Patroclus and weeping in a clear voice;
sentences.n: The subject of εὗρε ‘found’ is still Thetis. περικείμενον ‘lying round’ is the participle of περίκειμαι and takes the dative Πατρόκλῳ, so Achilles is stretched over the dead man’s body. ὃν φίλον υἱόν ‘her own dear son’: ὅν is the possessive ὅς ‘her own’, not the relative. κλαίοντα ‘weeping’ agrees with υἱόν, and λιγέως ‘clearly, in a clear voice’ is the house rendering. This unit ends in the middle of line 5.

sentences.t:
πολέες δ’ ἀμφ’ αὐτὸν ἑταῖροι
μύρονθ’·
sentences.l:
and many companions around him
were lamenting;
sentences.i: and many companions were lamenting around him;
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 5 and ends in the middle of line 6. πολέες is the epic form of πολλοί ‘many’, and ἀμφ’ αὐτόν ‘around him’ means round Achilles. μύρονθ’ is μύροντο, the imperfect middle of μύρομαι ‘lament’, in the plural to agree with ἑταῖροι ‘companions’.

sentences.t:
ἣ δ’ ἐν τοῖσι παρίστατο δῖα θεάων,
ἔν τ’ ἄρα οἱ φῦ χειρὶ ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζε·
sentences.l:
And she among them stood beside, heavenly-one of goddesses,
and clasped him by the hand, and spoke a word, and called him by name:
sentences.i: and she stood beside him among them, heavenly even among goddesses. She took his hand, and spoke, calling him by name:
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 6. ἣ δ’ is Thetis again, and παρίστατο is the imperfect middle of παρίστημι ‘stand beside’. δῖα θεάων ‘heavenly one of goddesses’ is a stock phrase, with the epic genitive plural θεάων. Line 7 is a formula for taking someone by the hand to speak: ἔν … φῦ is the aorist of ἐμφύω ‘cling to’ with its preverb separated from it, οἱ ‘to him’ is a dative and χειρί ‘by the hand’ names the hold, and ἔκ … ὀνόμαζε is split the same way. The unit joins the two so that line 6 is not left hanging on a comma.

sentences.t:
τέκνον ἐμὸν τοῦτον μὲν ἐάσομεν ἀχνύμενοί περ
κεῖσθαι, ἐπεὶ δὴ πρῶτα θεῶν ἰότητι δαμάσθη·
sentences.l:
“My child, this one we will let, though we grieve,
lie, since first by the will of the gods he was subdued;
sentences.i: “My child, we will let this man lie, grieving though we are, since to begin with it was by the will of the gods that he was brought down;
sentences.n: Thetis speaks. τέκνον ἐμόν ‘my child’ is a vocative, which in a neuter noun has the same form as the nominative. τοῦτον ‘this one’ is Patroclus, and μέν looks forward to τύνη δέ ‘but you’ in line 10. ἐάσομεν is a future, ‘we will let’, with the infinitive κεῖσθαι ‘lie’; the plural includes Thetis and Achilles, and ἀχνύμενοί περ means ‘though grieving’. δαμάσθη, the aorist passive of δαμάζω ‘subdue’, is the Homeric verb for being brought down by death; θεῶν ἰότητι ‘by the will of the gods’ is a dative of cause, with ἰότης as the house ‘will’. πρῶτα ‘first’ is an adverb, ‘to begin with’.
sentences.mark: Thetis tells Achilles to take the arms

sentences.t:
τύνη δ’ Ἡφαίστοιο πάρα κλυτὰ τεύχεα δέξο
καλὰ μάλ’, οἷ’ οὔ πώ τις ἀνὴρ ὤμοισι φόρησεν.
sentences.l:
but you, from Hephaestus the famous armour receive,
very fair, such as no man yet on his shoulders has borne.”
sentences.i: but you, take from Hephaestus the famous armour, very fair, such as no man has yet carried on his shoulders.”
sentences.n: τύνη is an emphatic epic form of σύ ‘you’. δέξο is the aorist imperative middle of δέχομαι ‘receive’ (Attic δέξαι), and Ἡφαίστοιο πάρα is παρὰ Ἡφαίστοιο ‘from Hephaestus’, with the accent drawn back as in θεοῦ πάρα at line 3. κλυτά ‘famous’ and καλά ‘fair’ agree with τεύχεα ‘armour’, a neuter plural. οἷα ‘such as’ introduces the description; οὔ πώ τις ἀνήρ is ‘no man yet’, ὤμοισι ‘on his shoulders’ is a dative plural, and φόρησεν is the aorist of φορέω ‘carry, wear’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὡς ἄρα φωνήσασα θεὰ κατὰ τεύχε’ ἔθηκε
πρόσθεν Ἀχιλλῆος·
sentences.l:
So then, having spoken, the goddess the armour set down
before Achilles;
sentences.i: With these words the goddess set the armour down before Achilles;
sentences.n: The line begins a new paragraph. ὡς ἄρα φωνήσασα (printed ὡς here, ὣς at line 37) is the stock phrase ‘so saying’, an aorist participle of φωνέω. κατὰ … ἔθηκε is tmesis, the preverb standing apart from the verb: ‘set down’, aorist of τίθημι. τεύχε’ is τεύχεα elided, and πρόσθεν ‘in front of’ takes the genitive Ἀχιλλῆος. This unit ends in the middle of line 13.

sentences.t: τὰ δ’ ἀνέβραχε δαίδαλα πάντα.
sentences.l: and they rang out, all the intricate works.
sentences.i: and all the intricate work rang out.
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 13. τά ‘they’ means the pieces of armour, and a neuter plural subject takes a singular verb in Greek, as ἀνέβραχε does here. ἀνέβραχε is the aorist of ἀναβράχω ‘clang, ring out’ (ἀνα- ‘up, aloud’). δαίδαλα πάντα ‘all the intricate works’ is the house rendering of δαίδαλα and stands in apposition to τά.

sentences.t:
Μυρμιδόνας δ’ ἄρα πάντας ἕλε τρόμος, οὐδέ τις ἔτλη
ἄντην εἰσιδέειν, ἀλλ’ ἔτρεσαν.
sentences.l:
And the Myrmidons all then trembling seized, and no one dared
to look at it face to face, but they shrank in fear.
sentences.i: A trembling took hold of all the Myrmidons, and no one dared to look straight at it, but they shrank away.
sentences.n: The Myrmidons are Achilles’ own men. ἕλε is the unaugmented aorist of αἱρέω ‘take, seize’ and has the accusative Μυρμιδόνας as its object, with τρόμος ‘trembling’ as subject. τις ἔτλη ‘anyone dared’ is the aorist of τλάω; ἄντην is the adverb ‘face to face’ and εἰσιδέειν the epic aorist infinitive of εἰσοράω ‘look at’. ἔτρεσαν is the aorist of τρέω ‘tremble, shrink in fear’. This unit ends in the middle of line 15.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀχιλλεὺς
ὡς εἶδ’, ὥς μιν μᾶλλον ἔδυ χόλος, ἐν δέ οἱ ὄσσε
δεινὸν ὑπὸ βλεφάρων ὡς εἰ σέλας ἐξεφάανθεν·
sentences.i: But when Achilles saw it, anger entered him all the more, and his eyes blazed terribly from under his lids like a flame;
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 15. αὐτάρ sets Achilles against the Myrmidons. ὡς εἶδ’ is ‘when he saw’ (ὡς temporal, εἶδ’ = εἶδε), and ὥς μιν μᾶλλον ἔδυ χόλος is ‘so anger entered him the more’: ἔδυ is the aorist of δύω ‘enter, sink into’ in its intransitive use, and χόλος is the house ‘anger’, not μῆνις. ὄσσε ‘eyes’ is a dual noun with the plural verb ἐξεφάανθεν, the epic aorist passive of ἐκφαίνω ‘show forth, blaze out’; οἱ ‘in him’ is a dative. ὡς εἰ σέλας is ‘as if a flame’.

sentences.t: τέρπετο δ’ ἐν χείρεσσιν ἔχων θεοῦ ἀγλαὰ δῶρα.
sentences.l: and he took delight, holding in his hands the splendid gifts of the god.
sentences.i: and he took delight in holding the god’s splendid gifts in his hands.
sentences.n: Achilles is still the subject. τέρπετο is the imperfect middle of τέρπομαι ‘take delight’, and ἔχων ‘holding’ is a present participle. ἐν χείρεσσιν ‘in his hands’ has the epic dative plural -εσσι. θεοῦ is Hephaestus, and ἀγλαά ‘splendid’ is the house word.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ φρεσὶν ᾗσι τετάρπετο δαίδαλα λεύσσων
αὐτίκα μητέρα ἣν ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
But when in his own wits he had taken his pleasure, gazing at the intricate works,
at once to his own mother winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: But when he had taken his pleasure in his wits, gazing at the intricate work, at once he spoke winged words to his own mother:
sentences.n: τετάρπετο is the reduplicated aorist of τέρπομαι, the verb of line 18: ‘he had taken his pleasure’. φρεσὶν ᾗσι ‘in his own wits’: ᾗσι is the possessive ὅς in the dative plural, ‘his own’, not the relative, and μητέρα ἣν ‘his own mother’ is the same possessive. δαίδαλα is the object of λεύσσων ‘gazing at’. ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα ‘spoke winged words to’ is the stock speech-introduction; μητέρα is its object, set before it.

sentences.t:
μῆτερ ἐμὴ τὰ μὲν ὅπλα θεὸς πόρεν οἷ’ ἐπιεικὲς
ἔργ’ ἔμεν ἀθανάτων, μὴ δὲ βροτὸν ἄνδρα τελέσσαι.
sentences.l:
“Mother mine, these arms the god has given, such as it is fitting
should be works of the immortals, and not that a mortal man finish.
sentences.i: “Mother, the god has given me armour such as it is fitting should be the work of immortals, and not for a mortal man to finish.
sentences.n: Achilles speaks. μῆτερ ἐμή ‘mother mine’ is a vocative. τὰ μὲν ὅπλα ‘these arms’ uses the article as a demonstrative, and μέν is answered by νῦν δέ in line 23. θεός is Hephaestus and πόρεν is the unaugmented aorist of πόρον ‘gave’. οἷα ‘such as’ is followed by ἐπιεικές ‘fitting’ and the infinitive ἔμεν (= εἶναι), ‘it is fitting that they be works of the immortals’; μὴ δὲ βροτὸν ἄνδρα τελέσσαι ‘and not that a mortal man finish them’ gives the accusative and infinitive (τελέσσαι, epic aorist of τελέω ‘finish’).

sentences.t: νῦν δ’ ἤτοι μὲν ἐγὼ θωρήξομαι·
sentences.l: But now, truly, I for my part shall arm myself;
sentences.i: But now I shall arm myself;
sentences.n: This unit ends in the middle of line 23. νῦν δέ answers the τὰ μέν of line 21: the arms are the god’s, but the arming is his own. ἤτοι ‘truly’ is printed as one word, and θωρήξομαι is the future middle of θωρήσσω ‘arm’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ μάλ’ αἰνῶς
δείδω μή μοι τόφρα Μενοιτίου ἄλκιμον υἱὸν
μυῖαι καδδῦσαι κατὰ χαλκοτύπους ὠτειλὰς
εὐλὰς ἐγγείνωνται, ἀεικίσσωσι δὲ νεκρόν,
ἐκ δ’ αἰὼν πέφαται, κατὰ δὲ χρόα πάντα σαπήῃ.
sentences.l:
but very dreadfully
I fear lest for me meanwhile in Menoetius’ sturdy son
flies, having sunk down through the bronze-struck wounds,
breed maggots, and disfigure the corpse —
out of him life has been killed — and down all his skin he rot.”
sentences.i: but I am dreadfully afraid that meanwhile flies will creep down into the bronze-struck wounds and breed maggots in the sturdy son of Menoetius, and disfigure the corpse — the life has been killed out of him — and that all his flesh will rot away.”
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 23. δείδω μή ‘I fear lest’ takes the subjunctives that follow, and μοι ‘for me’ shows the fear is his own. τόφρα is ‘meanwhile’. Μενοιτίου ἄλκιμον υἱόν is Patroclus, ‘sturdy’ being the house word for ἄλκιμος, and the accusative is the body in which the maggots breed (ἐγγείνωνται, aorist subjunctive middle of ἐγγείνομαι ‘breed in’). καδδῦσαι is κατα- + δῦσαι, ‘having sunk down’, with κατὰ … ὠτειλάς ‘through the wounds’, and χαλκοτύπους means ‘struck by bronze’. ἀεικίσσωσι is the aorist subjunctive of ἀεικίζω ‘disfigure’. ἐκ … πέφαται is a perfect passive indicative of φένω ‘slay’ (house ‘has been killed’, as at 17.689), with its preverb ἐκ standing apart: ‘life has been killed out of him’. It is not a subjunctive, so it is not one of the feared events but a plain statement that he is already dead, which the English sets between dashes. σαπήῃ is the aorist subjunctive passive of σήπω ‘rot’, and κατὰ … χρόα πάντα is κατά with the accusative, ‘down all his skin’ (χρώς is ‘skin’; the free layer says ‘flesh’ of the whole body); the subject of σαπήῃ is the body, ‘he rot’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα θεὰ Θέτις ἀργυρόπεζα·
sentences.l: Him then answered the goddess Thetis, silver-footed:
sentences.i: Then the goddess Thetis, silver-footed, answered him:
sentences.n: A whole-line reply formula, with the epithet ἀργυρόπεζα ‘silver-footed’ that the poem gives Thetis and that is translated every time. τόν is Achilles, ‘him’, and ἠμείβετο is the imperfect of ἀμείβομαι ‘answer’. The line begins a new paragraph.

sentences.t: τέκνον μή τοι ταῦτα μετὰ φρεσὶ σῇσι μελόντων.
sentences.l: “Child, let not these things be a care to you in your wits.
sentences.i: “My child, do not let these things be a care to your wits.
sentences.n: Thetis answers. τέκνον ‘child’ is a vocative. μή … μελόντων is a prohibition in the third-person plural imperative of μέλω ‘be a care’: ‘let them not be a care’. τοι is σοι ‘to you’, and μετὰ φρεσὶ σῇσι is ‘in your wits’, with σῇσι the dative plural of σός ‘your’. ταῦτα ‘these things’ are the flies and the rot Achilles has just named.
sentences.mark: Thetis promises to guard the body

sentences.t:
τῷ μὲν ἐγὼ πειρήσω ἀλαλκεῖν ἄγρια φῦλα
μυίας, αἵ ῥά τε φῶτας ἀρηϊφάτους κατέδουσιν·
sentences.l:
For him, for my part, I shall try to ward off the savage tribes,
the flies, that are wont to devour war-slain men;
sentences.i: I shall try to keep off him the savage tribes of flies, which devour men killed in war;
sentences.n: τῷ ‘for him’ is Patroclus, a dative of advantage, and μέν is answered by ἀλλὰ σύ in line 34. πειρήσω is a future, ‘I shall try’, and ἀλαλκεῖν the second-aorist infinitive of ἀλέξω ‘ward off’, which takes the accusative of what is kept off: ἄγρια φῦλα ‘savage tribes’, with μυίας ‘flies’ in apposition. ἀρηϊφάτους ‘slain in war’ joins Ἄρης to the root of φένω ‘slay’. αἵ ῥά τε … κατέδουσιν ‘which devour’ has the particle τε that marks what happens as a rule.

sentences.t:
ἤν περ γὰρ κεῖταί γε τελεσφόρον εἰς ἐνιαυτόν,
αἰεὶ τῷ γ’ ἔσται χρὼς ἔμπεδος, ἢ καὶ ἀρείων.
sentences.l:
For even if he lie for a completion-bearing year,
always for him will his skin be firm, or even better.
sentences.i: for even if he lies there for a full year, his flesh will always stay firm, or even better.
sentences.n: ἤν περ is ἐάν περ ‘even if’, and κεῖταί is the subjunctive of κεῖμαι ‘lie’. τελεσφόρον εἰς ἐνιαυτόν is ‘for a completion-bearing year’, that is, for a full year. τῷ γ’ ‘for him’ is Patroclus again. ἔσται is the future of εἰμί; χρώς is ‘skin’ (the free layer says ‘flesh’ of a whole body), ἔμπεδος ‘firm’, and ἢ καὶ ἀρείων ‘or even better’ uses ἀρείων, the comparative of ἀγαθός, agreeing with χρώς; it is ‘better’ here, not ‘braver’ as it is of a man’s courage at 2.707.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σύ γ’ εἰς ἀγορὴν καλέσας ἥρωας Ἀχαιοὺς
μῆνιν ἀποειπὼν Ἀγαμέμνονι ποιμένι λαῶν
αἶψα μάλ’ ἐς πόλεμον θωρήσσεο, δύσεο δ’ ἀλκήν.
sentences.l:
But you, to the assembly having called the hero Achaeans,
having renounced your wrath towards Agamemnon, shepherd of the people,
very quickly arm yourself for war, and put on might.”
sentences.i: But you, call the Achaean heroes to assembly, renounce your wrath towards Agamemnon, shepherd of the people, and very quickly arm yourself for war and put on might.”
sentences.n: ἀλλὰ σύ γ’ ‘but you’ answers the τῷ μέν of line 30, and the two aorist participles καλέσας ‘having called’ and ἀποειπών ‘having renounced’ lead up to the imperatives θωρήσσεο (present middle, ‘arm yourself’) and δύσεο (aorist middle of δύω ‘put on, enter into’, with ἀλκήν ‘might’ as object). ἀποειπών (ἀπο- ‘away’ + εἶπον ‘say’, ‘say off’) takes the accusative μῆνιν ‘wrath’, which is the house word, and the dative Ἀγαμέμνονι, which can be the man the wrath is against or the man to whom it is renounced, and ‘towards’ keeps both open; ποιμένι λαῶν ‘shepherd of the people’ is Agamemnon’s epithet. The line is metrically irregular as transmitted: the short syllable -πο- of ἀποειπών has to be counted long, as the longum of the second foot. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσασα μένος πολυθαρσὲς ἐνῆκε,
Πατρόκλῳ δ’ αὖτ’ ἀμβροσίην καὶ νέκταρ ἐρυθρὸν
στάξε κατὰ ῥινῶν, ἵνα οἱ χρὼς ἔμπεδος εἴη.
sentences.l:
So then, having spoken, much-daring strength she put in him,
and for Patroclus, in turn, ambrosia and red nectar
she dripped down into the nostrils, so that his skin might be firm.
sentences.i: With these words she put strength of great daring into him, and in turn she dripped ambrosia and red nectar down Patroclus’ nostrils, so that his flesh might stay firm.
sentences.n: The line begins a new paragraph. ὣς ἄρα φωνήσασα is the stock ‘so saying’, and ἐνῆκε is the aorist of ἐνίημι ‘put in’, with μένος πολυθαρσές ‘strength of great daring’ as its object (the Odyssey has the phrase at 13.387); the one who receives the strength is Achilles. Πατρόκλῳ is a dative of the person helped, στάξε the aorist of στάζω ‘drip’, and κατὰ ῥινῶν ‘down the nostrils’, with ῥινῶν the genitive plural of ῥίς. ἀμβροσίη and νέκταρ are the food and drink of the gods; ἐρυθρόν is ‘red’. ἵνα with the optative εἴη gives purpose, and ἔμπεδος is ‘firm’ again, said of the χρώς ‘skin’ (‘flesh’ in the free layer).

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὃ βῆ παρὰ θῖνα θαλάσσης δῖος Ἀχιλλεὺς
σμερδαλέα ἰάχων, ὦρσεν δ’ ἥρωας Ἀχαιούς.
sentences.l:
But he went along the shore of the sea, heavenly Achilles,
crying out terribly, and roused the hero Achaeans.
sentences.i: But heavenly Achilles went along the shore of the sea, crying out terribly, and roused the Achaean heroes.
sentences.n: The line begins a new paragraph. ὁ ‘he’ is Achilles, picked up by the stock δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς ‘heavenly Achilles’. βῆ is ἔβη without the augment, and παρὰ θῖνα ‘along the beach’. σμερδαλέα ἰάχων ‘crying out terribly’ has a neuter plural adverb and a participle of ἰάχω ‘cry out’. ὦρσεν is the aorist of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’; ἥρωας Ἀχαιούς is ‘the hero Achaeans’.

sentences.t:
καί ῥ’ οἵ περ τὸ πάρος γε νεῶν ἐν ἀγῶνι μένεσκον
οἵ τε κυβερνῆται καὶ ἔχον οἰήϊα νηῶν
καὶ ταμίαι παρὰ νηυσὶν ἔσαν σίτοιο δοτῆρες,
καὶ μὴν οἳ τότε γ’ εἰς ἀγορὴν ἴσαν, οὕνεκ’ Ἀχιλλεὺς
ἐξεφάνη, δηρὸν δὲ μάχης ἐπέπαυτ’ ἀλεγεινῆς.
sentences.l:
And those who indeed formerly in the gathering of the ships used to stay,
those who were helmsmen and held the steering-oars of ships,
and stewards by the ships, who were givers of food,
even these then went to the assembly, because Achilles
had appeared, and for long from grievous fighting had ceased.
sentences.i: Even those who in the past used to stay in the gathering-place of the ships — the helmsmen who held the ships’ steering-oars, and the stewards beside the ships who gave out the food — even they went to the assembly then, because Achilles had appeared, after long ceasing from grievous fighting.
sentences.n: One long sentence, whose subjects pile up before its verb ἴσαν ‘went’ in line 45. οἵ περ τὸ πάρος … μένεσκον ‘those who formerly used to stay’: μένεσκον is an iterative imperfect of μένω, and νεῶν ἐν ἀγῶνι ‘in the gathering of the ships’ means the camp itself, ἀγών being a place of gathering. οἵ τε κυβερνῆται καὶ ἔχον οἰήϊα νηῶν is ‘who were helmsmen and held the steering-oars of ships’, and καὶ ταμίαι … σίτοιο δοτῆρες ‘and stewards, givers of food’ adds a second class of men who had not left the ships. ἔσαν is ἦσαν; καὶ μὴν is ‘yes, and’; ἴσαν is the imperfect of εἶμι ‘go’. The clause from οὕνεκ’ on repeats words of Book 18, said there of the Trojans: ἐξεφάνη ‘appeared’, and ἐπέπαυτ’ is the pluperfect middle of παύω ‘had ceased’, with the genitive μάχης.

sentences.t:
τὼ δὲ δύω σκάζοντε βάτην Ἄρεος θεράποντε
Τυδεΐδης τε μενεπτόλεμος καὶ δῖος Ὀδυσσεὺς
ἔγχει ἐρειδομένω·
sentences.i: And the two attendants of Ares, the son of Tydeus, steadfast in battle, and heavenly Odysseus, went limping, leaning on their spears;
sentences.n: τὼ δὲ δύω ‘and the two’ opens a run of duals: σκάζοντε ‘limping’, βάτην ‘went’ (the dual of the aorist of βαίνω), θεράποντε ‘attendants’ and ἐρειδομένω ‘leaning’. Ἄρεος θεράποντε ‘attendants of Ares’ means warriors. Τυδεΐδης ‘Tydeus’-son’ is Diomedes, not named, with the stock μενεπτόλεμος ‘steadfast in battle’; the other is δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς ‘heavenly Odysseus’. Both were wounded in Book 11. ἔγχει is a singular dative, one spear for each man. This unit ends in the middle of line 49.

sentences.t: ἔτι γὰρ ἔχον ἕλκεα λυγρά·
sentences.l: for still they had wounds, grievous ones;
sentences.i: for they still had grievous wounds;
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 49 and gives the reason for the spears. ἔτι ‘still’, ἔχον the imperfect of ἔχω, and ἕλκεα the epic plural of ἕλκος ‘wound’, with λυγρά ‘grievous’.

sentences.t: κὰδ δὲ μετὰ πρώτῃ ἀγορῇ ἵζοντο κιόντες.
sentences.l: and down among the first of the assembly they sat, going in.
sentences.i: and they went and sat down at the front of the assembly.
sentences.n: κὰδ δέ is κατὰ δέ, with κατά assimilated to the δ; it is in tmesis with ἵζοντο ‘sat down’. μετὰ πρώτῃ ἀγορῇ is literally ‘among the first assembly’, taken as the foremost part of the gathering; κιόντες is the participle of κίω ‘go’, here ‘going in’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὃ δεύτατος ἦλθεν ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων
ἕλκος ἔχων·
sentences.l:
But he last came, lord of men, Agamemnon,
having a wound;
sentences.i: Last of all came Agamemnon, lord of men, with his wound;
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὅ ‘but he’ is Agamemnon, named only at the end of the line. δεύτατος ‘last’ is a superlative of δεύτερος, and ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν ‘lord of men’ is the stock epithet. ἕλκος ἔχων ‘having a wound’ was got in Book 11. This unit ends in the middle of line 52.

sentences.t:
καὶ γὰρ τὸν ἐνὶ κρατερῇ ὑσμίνῃ
οὖτα Κόων Ἀντηνορίδης χαλκήρεϊ δουρί.
sentences.l:
for indeed him in strong battle
wounded Coön, Antenor’s-son, with a bronze-fitted spear.
sentences.i: for Coön, son of Antenor, had wounded him in strong battle with a bronze-fitted spear.
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 52. καὶ γάρ ‘for indeed’ gives the reason for the wound, and τόν ‘him’ is Agamemnon. ἐνὶ κρατερῇ ὑσμίνῃ ‘in strong battle’ and χαλκήρεϊ δουρί ‘with a bronze-fitted spear’ are house phrases; οὖτα is the aorist of οὐτάω ‘wound with a thrust’. Ἀντηνορίδης is a patronymic, ‘Antenor’s son’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δὴ πάντες ἀολλίσθησαν Ἀχαιοί,
τοῖσι δ’ ἀνιστάμενος μετέφη πόδας ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.l:
But when indeed all the Achaeans had been gathered together,
among them, standing up, spoke swift-in-feet Achilles:
sentences.i: When all the Achaeans were gathered together, Achilles, swift of foot, stood up among them and spoke:
sentences.n: ἀολλίσθησαν is the aorist passive of ἀολλίζω ‘gather together’, from ἀολλής ‘in a throng’. Line 55 is the stock introduction to Achilles’ speech: τοῖσι ‘to them’, ἀνιστάμενος ‘standing up’, μετέφη ‘spoke among’ and πόδας ὠκύς ‘swift in feet’.

sentences.l:
“Atreus’-son, truly then, in any way, this for both of us better
was it, for you and me, that we two, though grieving at heart,
in heart-devouring strife were eager on account of a girl?
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, was this after all any better for the two of us, for you and for me, that we, though grieving at heart, were eager in heart-devouring strife for the sake of a girl?
sentences.n: Achilles speaks to Agamemnon. Ἀτρεΐδη ‘son of Atreus’ is a vocative, and ἦ ἄρ τι opens a question, ‘was it then in any way…’. τόδ’ ‘this’ is the quarrel; ἀμφοτέροισιν ‘for both’ is a dative, ἄρειον ‘better’ is the neuter comparative of ἀγαθός (as ἀρείων at line 33), ‘more to the good’, with ἔπλετο ‘it was, it proved’. ὅ τε ‘that’ introduces what was supposedly better. νῶΐ ‘we two’, ἀχνυμένω ‘grieving’ and κῆρ ‘at heart’ (an accusative of respect) go together, and μενεήναμεν is the aorist of μενεαίνω ‘be eager’, the house rendering; the verb has no object here, and the strife it was spent in is the dative ἔριδι. θυμοβόρῳ ἔριδι is ‘in heart-devouring strife’ and εἵνεκα κούρης ‘for the sake of a girl’, Briseis, unnamed. The Greek question mark ends the unit.

sentences.t:
τὴν ὄφελ’ ἐν νήεσσι κατακτάμεν Ἄρτεμις ἰῷ
ἤματι τῷ ὅτ’ ἐγὼν ἑλόμην Λυρνησσὸν ὀλέσσας·
sentences.l:
Her, would that Artemis had killed among the ships with an arrow
on that day when I took Lyrnessus, destroying it;
sentences.i: Would that Artemis had killed her with an arrow among the ships on the day I took Lyrnessus and destroyed it;
sentences.n: τὴν ‘her’ is the girl. ὄφελ’ is ὄφελε(ν), the unaugmented past of ὀφέλλω (Attic ὤφελε), which with an infinitive expresses a wish that cannot now be met: ‘would that she had killed’, κατακτάμεν being the epic aorist infinitive of κατακτείνω. Artemis is the goddess whose arrows bring sudden death to women. ἐν νήεσσι ‘among the ships’ has the epic dative plural, and ἰῷ is the dative of ἰός ‘arrow’. ἤματι τῷ ὅτ’ is ‘on that day when’; ἐγών is the epic form of ἐγώ; ἑλόμην is the aorist middle of αἱρέω ‘take (for myself)’, and ὀλέσσας the aorist participle of ὄλλυμι ‘destroy’. Lyrnessus is the town where Briseis was taken.

sentences.t:
τώ κ’ οὐ τόσσοι Ἀχαιοὶ ὀδὰξ ἕλον ἄσπετον οὖδας
δυσμενέων ὑπὸ χερσὶν ἐμεῦ ἀπομηνίσαντος.
sentences.l:
then not so many Achaeans with their teeth would have bitten the boundless ground
under the hands of enemies, I having withdrawn in wrath.
sentences.i: then not so many Achaeans would have bitten the boundless earth with their teeth under the hands of enemies, when I had withdrawn in wrath.
sentences.n: τώ is τῷ ‘in that case’, and κ’ with the aorist ἕλον makes the unreal ‘would have bitten’. ὀδὰξ ἕλον οὖδας is the formula for falling dead, ‘bit the ground with their teeth’, with ἄσπετον ‘boundless’. δυσμενέων is the epic genitive plural of δυσμενής ‘hostile’, used as ‘enemies’, and ὑπὸ χερσίν ‘under the hands’ takes the dative. ἐμεῦ ἀπομηνίσαντος is a genitive absolute, ‘I having withdrawn in wrath’: ἐμεῦ is the epic genitive of ἐγώ and ἀπομηνίσαντος the aorist participle of ἀπομηνίω; the force of ἀπο- (‘away’, ‘to the end’) is not certain.

sentences.t: Ἕκτορι μὲν καὶ Τρωσὶ τὸ κέρδιον·
sentences.l: For Hector and the Trojans, the better thing;
sentences.i: That was the better thing for Hector and the Trojans;
sentences.n: This unit ends in the middle of line 63. There is no verb in the Greek; ‘was’ is understood. τὸ κέρδιον is ‘the better thing’, a comparative built on κέρδος ‘gain’ and so ‘better’ in the sense of more to one’s profit; it means what in fact happened, the quarrel and its cost, and μέν is answered by αὐτάρ in the next unit.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀχαιοὺς
δηρὸν ἐμῆς καὶ σῆς ἔριδος μνήσεσθαι ὀΐω.
sentences.l:
but the Achaeans
for long of my strife and yours will be mindful, I think.
sentences.i: but I think the Achaeans will remember for a long time the strife of you and me.
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 63. Ἀχαιούς is the accusative subject of the future infinitive μνήσεσθαι ‘will remember’, which takes the genitive ἔριδος, after ὀΐω ‘I think’. δηρόν is ‘for a long time’, and ἐμῆς καὶ σῆς ‘mine and yours’ are two possessive adjectives agreeing with ἔριδος.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ τὰ μὲν προτετύχθαι ἐάσομεν ἀχνύμενοί περ,
θυμὸν ἐνὶ στήθεσσι φίλον δαμάσαντες ἀνάγκῃ·
sentences.l:
But those things, done now and past, we will let be, though we grieve,
having subdued the dear heart in our breasts by necessity;
sentences.i: But what is done and past we will let be, grieving though we are, mastering the heart in our breasts by necessity;
sentences.n: These two lines are the same as 18.112–113, where Achilles first spoke of giving up his anger; here he says it before the assembly. προτετύχθαι is the perfect passive infinitive of προτεύχω, ‘to have been done before’, so τὰ μὲν προτετύχθαι is ‘the things already done’. ἐάσομεν is a future, ‘we will let be’, with the plural of Achilles speaking of himself; ἀχνύμενοί περ is ‘though grieving’. δαμάσαντες is the aorist participle of δαμάζω ‘subdue’, and ἀνάγκῃ ‘by necessity’ is a dative of means.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ἤτοι μὲν ἐγὼ παύω χόλον, οὐδέ τί με χρὴ
ἀσκελέως αἰεὶ μενεαινέμεν·
sentences.l:
But now, truly, I for my part stop my anger, and there is no need for me
stubbornly always to be eager;
sentences.i: But now I stop my anger; and there is no need for me to go on being eager, stubbornly, for ever;
sentences.n: The opening is the one of line 23, νῦν δ’ ἤτοι μὲν ἐγώ. παύω ‘I stop’ is a present with χόλος ‘anger’ as object. οὐδέ τί με χρή is ‘and there is no need for me’, with the accusative με and the infinitive μενεαινέμεν (= μενεαίνειν, ‘to be eager’, the house rendering, again with no object). The sense of ἀσκελέως is not certain: it is an adverb from ἀσκελής ‘dried-up, hard’ (‘withered’ in the Odyssey), and ‘stubbornly’ is a guess from the context, with αἰεί ‘always’ beside it. This unit ends in the middle of line 68.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε θᾶσσον
ὄτρυνον πόλεμον δὲ κάρη κομόωντας Ἀχαιούς,
ὄφρ’ ἔτι καὶ Τρώων πειρήσομαι ἀντίον ἐλθὼν
αἴ κ’ ἐθέλωσ’ ἐπὶ νηυσὶν ἰαύειν·
sentences.l:
but come, more quickly
urge on to war the long-haired-of-head Achaeans,
so that I may yet try the Trojans too, having gone to meet them,
if they are willing to sleep beside the ships;
sentences.i: but come, quickly urge the long-haired Achaeans on to war, so that I may yet try the Trojans too, going to meet them, to see if they are willing to sleep beside the ships;
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 68 and ends in the middle of line 71. ἀλλ’ ἄγε is ‘but come’, and θᾶσσον, a comparative, is used as ‘quickly’. ὄτρυνον is an imperative of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’, spoken to Agamemnon; πόλεμον δέ is ‘to war’, with the ending -δε of motion towards; κάρη κομόωντας Ἀχαιούς is the stock ‘long-haired Achaeans’. ὄφρα (ὄφρ’) with the future πειρήσομαι gives purpose, ‘so that I may try’, and takes the genitive Τρώων; ἀντίον ἐλθών is ‘having gone to meet them’. αἴ κ’ is εἰ κε ‘if perhaps’, and ἰαύειν is ‘to sleep’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά τιν’ οἴω
ἀσπασίως αὐτῶν γόνυ κάμψειν, ὅς κε φύγῃσι
δηΐου ἐκ πολέμοιο ὑπ’ ἔγχεος ἡμετέροιο.
sentences.l:
but I think some one of them
gladly will bend the knee, whoever may flee
from the hostile war, from under our spear.”
sentences.i: but I think that any of them who escapes from the hostile war and from under our spear will gladly bend his knee.”
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 71. ἀλλά τιν’ οἴω is ‘but I think that someone’, with the future infinitive κάμψειν ‘will bend’ and αὐτῶν ‘of them’ (the Trojans) naming the group. γόνυ κάμψειν ‘bend the knee’ is usually understood as taking rest; the Greek says only ‘bend the knee’. ἀσπασίως is ‘gladly’. ὅς κε φύγῃσι is ‘whoever escapes’ (aorist subjunctive with κε); δηΐου ‘hostile’ goes with πολέμοιο ‘war’, and ὑπ’ ἔγχεος ἡμετέροιο is ‘from under our spear’, with the epic ending -οιο. The speech ends here, and the part with it.
